# **1\. Context and data scope**

The data describes a consumer-electronics retailer operating in Melbourne: it covers ten product categories, from accessories to laptops, with every customer address in Victoria and every price in Australian dollars. Goods leave three warehouses, carried by four carriers offering two service levels, and customers can buy through three channels — web, mobile and in store.

The metadata in each file names its source: a JSON export from `CommercePlatform` and an XML export from `OperationsERP`, both holding 2018 data. Neither file is complete on its own — customer records exist only in the JSON file, and the product catalogue only in the XML file — so the analytical tables are built by combining the two files rather than choosing one of them. They overlap with each other, repeat rows internally, and their formats differ but their values do not, a match we return to in section 6\.

The data covers 5,000 orders placed between 1 January and 31 December 2018 by 500 customers (the period is defined by order date, since some deliveries ran into January 2019). It sits in six tables. `orders` and `deliveries` hold 5,000 rows each — one per order, one per its delivery. `order_items` holds 15,685 rows, one per item, with one to five items per order. `customers` holds 500 rows and `products` 1,000. `product_reviews` holds 7,000 rows, one per reviewed item, covering 3,993 of the 5,000 orders (customers choose whether to review).

# **2\. Data-preparation assurance**   

Four data-preparation decisions govern the analytical tables. They define table grain, monetary calculations and text handling; every downstream figure depends on them. All tables were built and analysed in Python with pandas (The pandas development team, 2024\) and matplotlib (Hunter, 2007).

1. **Canonical rows via pre-deduplication normalisation.**

Source files supply all transactional tables. Rows are concatenated, normalised to a common format, and reduced to one row per key via first-wins deduplication (`MAP-orders-01`). Order of operations is critical: deduplicating before normalising treats `25/12/2018` and `2018-12-25` as separate orders and retains both. Every analytical grain—order, order item, delivery, and review—relies on this sequence, and key uniqueness is re-verified on every export.

2. **Sequential monetary recomputation.**

Derived fields are recomputed step-by-step rather than copied from source data:

`line_revenue = quantity × unit price` (`MAP-order_items-06`)  
`order_price = sum of line revenues` (`MAP-orders-10`)  
`order_total = order_price × (1 − coupon_discount ÷ 100) + delivery charges` (`MAP-orders-15`)  
`tax_amount = round(order_price / 11, 2)` (`MAP-orders-14`)

    Coupons apply as percentage points to goods before adding delivery charges (`MAP-orders-13`); reversing this order alters final totals. Because listed prices include GST, tax is extracted rather than copied, preventing upstream arithmetic faults from propagating. Recomputed values reconcile against source data within a `0.01` tolerance.

3. **Text cleaning in a fixed order.**

 Product review text is cleaned while preserving non-Latin characters (`MAP-product_reviews-10`). Embedded identifiers are extracted before cleaning strips formatting wrappers (`MAP-product_reviews-17`, `MAP-product_reviews-18`). Latin-only length metrics are calculated post-cleaning (`MAP-product_reviews-11`).

4. **Deliberate non-transformation of the delivery note.**

`delivery_note_clean` is copied unchanged (`MAP-deliveries-20`) because it contains only two structured values: `Delivered within promise` (4,472 rows) and `Carrier scan reconciled` (528 rows) across all 5,000 canonical deliveries. Applying the narrative cleaner would alter text cases across every row without adding analytical value.

Six validation results carry the assurance; each is recomputed in the notebook, not asserted.  **Grain holds.** All six primary keys are unique with no blanks, and each table's row count equals the number of different keys the two files hold between them — 5,000 orders, 15,685 order items, 500 customers, 5,000 deliveries, 1,000 products, 7,000 reviews (VAL-PK, VAL-FLOW-01 to \-06).

**First-wins deduplication loses nothing.** It removes 68 rows from each file (VAL-FLOW-07), and across the six tables 8,098 rows carry a repeated key with 0 field disagreements after normalising, and 0 differences between the two copies of any within-file duplicate (VAL-FLOW-09, VAL-FLOW-10). No exported value depends on which copy was kept.

**Every join in this report resolves.**  All nine foreign keys return 0 unmatched values (VAL-FK-01 to \-09).

**The money chain reconciles.** Recomputed line revenue, order price, order total and tax each match the source within 0.01 on every row — 0 of 15,685 and 0 of 5,000 outside tolerance (VAL-ARITH-01 to \-04).

**Extraction ran before cleaning.** 7,000 order references were found and none survives in the cleaned text (VAL-TEXT-06), and none is wrong: 0 of 7,000 references disagree with their own order, 0 of 7,000 SKUs with their product (VAL-TEXT-14, VAL-TEXT-15).

**The literal NaN is a sentinel, not a gap.** coupon\_code and promo\_code carry it on the same 3,127 orders and no field mixes it with an empty cell (VAL-TEXT-11), while the real word none in delay\_reason survives on 4,472 rows instead of being read as missing (VAL-TEXT-09).

# **3\. Assessed visualisations**

* Figure 1 — Univariate distribution

![][image1]

**Figure 1\.** Distribution of order value, with the median and mean marked. One row per order; all 5,000 orders. 

This figure asks how order value is distributed, and whether the mean misleads. The observation unit is one order; the denominator is all 5,000 canonical orders, from orders with no join. The distribution is strongly right-skewed: the median is AUD 2,502 against a mean of AUD 2,983, 19% higher, and the mean sits above 59% of orders. Values run from AUD 22 to AUD 17,720, the top 5% above AUD 7,135. A histogram rather than a boxplot, because the point is the shape of the tail and where the mean falls inside it. A typical order should be planned with the median. Limitation: order\_total is net of the coupon and includes delivery charges, so it is not basket size.

* Figure 2 — Bivariate relationship

![][image2]

**Figure 2\.** Revenue and unit sales by product category. One row per order line; all 15,685 lines. 

This figure evaluates whether the highest-revenue categories are also the highest-volume ones. The observation unit is one order line, and the denominator is all 15,685 canonical `order_items` rows, joined to `products` on `product_id` for each line's category. Revenue is summed at line grain; units sold is the sum of `quantity`, 20,154 items. Paired bar panels, because the comparison is a rank order across ten named categories.  
Revenue and volume rankings are near-inverses:

* **Laptops:** 1st in gross line revenue (AUD 2.75m), 9th in units (1,397).  
* **Accessories:** 1st in units (3,051), 10th in revenue (AUD 0.56m).

**Category revenue is driven by unit price rather than sales volume.** Maintaining strict data grain is critical: summing `order_total` post-join yields AUD 52.7m against the true AUD 14.9m—a 3.53× inflation caused by duplicating order-level totals across individual item lines.  
Limitation: `line_revenue` reflects gross figures. Order-level coupon discounts (AUD 1.62m total) reduce gross revenue from AUD 16.47m to AUD 14.85m invoiced. Because coupons apply as flat order-level percentages, attributing discounts to individual product categories requires unrecorded pro-rata assumptions.

* Figure 3 — Temporal pattern

![][image3]

**Figure 3\.** Monthly revenue split into order count and order size. One row per order; all 5,000 orders of 2018\. 

From orders alone, with no join. Three line panels stacked on one shared time axis, because revenue is the product of the other two and the question is which of them moves. Revenue barely moves. It stays between AUD 1.10m and 1.36m, varying 6.1% across the year. Neither half explains it: the number of orders varies 4.2% and the average order 4.0%, so they contribute about equally. Volume runs 384 to 443 orders a month. One year gives no second cycle to compare against, so we can describe the shape but cannot call it seasonal. 

* Figure 4 — Multivariate and operational

![][image4]

**Figure 4\.** On-time rate by carrier, service level and warehouse, with 95% Wilson intervals (Wilson, 1927). One row per delivery; all 5,000 deliveries. 

Deliveries joined to orders on order\_id, one to one, which is what supplies the warehouse and the delivery charge. Dot-and-interval rather than bars, because the result is that these rates cannot be told apart and bars would invite the reader to rank them. On-time performance is 89.4% and barely moves. All 24 combinations of carrier, service level and warehouse fall between 81.8% and 95.8%. Express reaches 89.7% against Standard's 89.4%, a gap of 0.3 points on 901 Express deliveries, and it does not even buy a shorter promise: 5.03 promised days against 4.99, at AUD 23.48 a delivery against Standard's AUD 12.17. 

Some combinations do look different — the Express-minus-Standard gap runs from −10.0 to \+7.0 points. But every Express group holds fewer than 100 deliveries, against 151 to 470 for Standard. Groups that small move around on their own, so those gaps are not evidence of a carrier effect.

* Figure 5 — Review and text behaviour

![][image5]

**Figure 5\.** Review length by rating, split into Latin-script and non-Latin-script reviews. One row per review; all 7,000 reviews. 

Figure 5 asks whether rating, review length and script are related. The unit is one review across all 7,000 reviews, from product\_reviews with no join. Boxplots on a log length scale, because lengths run from 180 to 2,492 characters and the spread inside each rating matters as much as its median. The 271 reviews containing non-Latin script have a median cleaned length of 607 characters, compared with 927 among 6,729 Latin-only reviews. Latin-only median length falls about 7%, from 980 characters at two stars to 907 at five, while the non-Latin group has no ordered pattern. The smaller non-Latin sample, language-specific writing conventions and cleaning rules limit interpretation; these results are descriptive, not causal.

* Figure 6 — Delivery performance

![][image6]

**Figure 6\.** Mean rating for on-time and late deliveries, with 95% confidence intervals. One row per review; all 7,000 reviews, joined to deliveries on `order_id`. 

This figure evaluates whether late deliveries attract lower ratings. The observation unit is one review, and the denominator is all 7,000 canonical product\_reviews joined to deliveries on order\_id to attach each review's delivery outcome. The join preserves all 7,000 rows because every review maps to exactly one delivery. Two means with their confidence intervals rather than bars, because the gap is small and its uncertainty is the finding.

Late deliveries (n \= 707\) average 3.82 stars against 3.70 for on-time deliveries (n \= 6,293). The 0.12-star gap is negligible on a 1–5 scale.

Two limitations apply. First, lateness is measured once, not twice. product\_reviews.delivery\_experience looks like the customer's own account of the delivery, but it takes only the values delayed (707) and on\_time (6,293) and agrees with deliveries.on\_time\_in\_full on all 7,000 rows, so it is the operational outcome relabelled. Second, only 7,000 of 15,685 delivered items carry a review, so the figure describes reviewers and not customers.

* Figure 7 — Segmented relationship

![][image7]

**Figure 7\.** Spend per customer split into how often they order and how much they spend each time. One row per customer; all 500 customers. 

This figure asks which customer segments spend the most, and whether any gap is about ordering more often or spending more each time. The observation unit is one customer; the denominator is all 500 customers — orders are summarised to one row per customer first, then joined to customers on customer\_id, so the join still returns 500 rows. The total is split into its two components on one figure, because they move in opposite directions and the total on its own hides that.

The four segments spend almost the same: Mainstream AUD 31,360 at the top, Small Business AUD 28,897 at the bottom — a gap of only 1.5 standard errors.

The two parts behind that total run opposite ways. Value orders 10.4 times at AUD 2,846 each; Small Business orders 9.4 times at AUD 3,062. Buying often and cheaply cancels buying rarely and dearly, so the totals match while the behaviour does not.

Limitation: customer\_segment is a label already in the data, and we do not know the rule behind it.

* Figure 8 — Multivariate relationship

![][image8]

**Figure 8\.** Rating and helpful votes by price quintile. One row per reviewed order item; all 7,000 reviews. 

Figure 8 asks whether unit price relates to rating and helpful votes. The unit is one reviewed order item: product\_reviews joined to order\_items on order\_item\_id and then to products on product\_id, both joins keeping the 7,000-row grain. Points with intervals rather than bars from zero, because the question is whether the quintiles differ by more than their own uncertainty. Mean rating falls from 3.879 in price quintile 1 to 3.548 in quintile 4, a 0.331-star drop of about seven standard errors, before rebounding to 3.684 in quintile 5\. Helpful-vote medians remain between 44.0 and 45.5 against within-quintile middle-half ranges of about 21–68. Only reviewed purchases are observed, and category mix may confound the price relationship.

# **4\. Ten findings**

* Finding 1

At the line-item level (15,685 lines), high sales volume does not necessarily mean high revenue. Laptops generate the most revenue (AUD 2.75m) despite ranking only 9th in units sold (1,397). In contrast, Accessories sell the most units (3,051) but generate the lowest revenue (AUD 0.56m). The pattern may be price level restated rather than any demand effect — a laptop costs many times what an accessory costs — and one year of one region cannot separate the two. Therefore, inventory and marketing decisions should not be based on sales volume alone. Once cost data is available, categories should also be compared by profit margin.

* Finding 2

Among reviewed items, late deliveries do not have lower ratings: they average 3.82 stars compared with 3.70 for on-time deliveries. This does not show that delays improve ratings or are harmless. Only reviewed items are observed, and unmeasured differences between orders or customers may explain the unexpected direction.

* Finding 3

Revenue is flat all year. At order grain across all 5,000 orders of 2018, monthly revenue sits between AUD 1.10m and 1.36m, a spread of 6.1%, and neither component drives it: order count varies 4.2% (384 to 443 a month) and mean order value 4.0%. Nothing in the twelve months reads as a peak to staff for or a trough to discount into. But the figure cannot rule seasonality out: one year gives no second cycle to compare against, and 5,000 orders over twelve months is thin. Keep monthly targets flat until a second year exists.   

* Finding 4

Nine in ten deliveries arrive on time — 89.4% of 5,000 — and nothing we can group by changes that. All 24 combinations of carrier, service level and warehouse land between 81.8% and 95.8%. Express is charged at AUD 23.48 a delivery against Standard's AUD 12.17, 93% more, for the same five-day promise (5.03 days against 4.99) and the same on-time rate (89.7% on 901 Express deliveries against 89.4% on 4,099). Some carriers show gaps of up to 10 points between the two, but every Express group holds fewer than 100 deliveries against 151 to 470 for Standard, and groups that small move on their own. The data holds what the customer pays, not what either service costs to run, and Express may cover harder routes — check both before touching the price.   

* Finding 5

At order grain across all 5,000 orders, the median is AUD 2,502 but the average is AUD 2,983 — higher than 59% of orders. The range runs AUD 22 to AUD 17,720, the top 5% above AUD 7,135. Quoting the average makes a typical order look about 20% bigger than it is, so packaging, delivery cost or a free-shipping threshold set from it would be sized for a customer who mostly does not exist. One caveat: order\_total includes delivery charges and is net of the coupon, so part of the spread is shipping, not goods. Plan with the median.

* Finding 6

At customer grain across all 500 customers, the four segments spend almost the same: Mainstream AUD 31,360 against Small Business AUD 28,897, only 1.5 standard errors apart on 110 to 139 customers each. The parts differ, in opposite directions: Value orders 10.4 times at AUD 2,846, Small Business 9.4 times at AUD 3,062, about 2.4 standard errors each. A campaign aimed at high-spending segments has nothing to aim at; one aimed at order frequency or basket size does. These are the largest of twelve comparisons, so treat them as a lead, and customer\_segment may itself have been assigned from earlier behaviour.

* Finding 7

At review grain across all 7,000 reviews, the 271 containing non-Latin script have a median cleaned length of 607 characters, compared with 927 for the 6,729 Latin-only reviews. Latin-only median length declines about 7% from two to five stars, while the smaller non-Latin group shows no ordered pattern. Review length should therefore not be used alone as a satisfaction signal. The result is descriptive rather than causal because language-specific writing conventions, text-cleaning rules and the much smaller non-Latin sample may account for part of the observed gap.

* Finding 8

At reviewed-order-item grain across 7,000 reviews, mean rating falls from 3.879 in the lowest price quintile to 3.548 in the fourth, a 0.331-star gap of roughly seven standard errors, then rebounds to 3.684 in the highest. Helpful-vote medians vary only from 44.0 to 45.5. Price alone is therefore unsuitable for targeting review interventions. The pattern is descriptive rather than causal because only 7,000 of 15,685 order lines have reviews and differences in product-category mix may partly explain the rating gap.

* Finding 9

Across the six tables, 8,098 rows carry a key that appears in both files or twice in one. Once the two formats are made the same, not one of those rows disagrees on any value (VAL-FLOW-09, VAL-FLOW-10). The check does work: before the formats were matched it found 7 columns disagreeing in orders alone, and all 3,500 of those differences were ways of writing a value — 25/12/2018 against 2018-12-25 — never the value itself. Two systems recording these orders separately would slip somewhere. One system exported twice is the simpler explanation, so the match shows nothing was damaged on the way out, not that either file is right.

* Finding 10

The deliveries table has five columns that all record whether a delivery was late. Four are obvious outcomes: delay\_reason, on\_time\_in\_full, delay\_days, and delivered\_date compared with promised\_date. The fifth, delivery\_note\_clean, splits all 5,000 deliveries into exactly the same two groups as the other four, with not one row disagreeing: 4,472 on time, 528 late, or 10.6%. It is an outcome too, written after delivery, but its name does not say so, which is why it is the one left in a model by mistake. It may also be that this is just how this one extract came out: two note values over one year cannot show whether the note is written from the outcome or only happens to match it. ML question 1 predicts lateness before dispatch, so keeping it lets the model read the answer. For now, no lateness model should use it.

# **5\. Five machine-learning questions**

* MLQ-1 Will this order be delivered later than promised?

*Classification · one order at placement · target: on\_time\_in\_full · train on earlier months, test on later*

*Figure 4 showed 528 of 5,000 deliveries arrive late, and no grouping clearly separates them — all 24 carrier, service level and warehouse groups fall between 81.8% and 95.8% — so a model needs subtler signals. Flagging orders before dispatch would let us warn customers or hold capacity, focusing on 528 rather than 5,000. At placement we know the timestamp, channel, carrier, service level, promised days, shipping distance, delivery cost, cart size and value. Score on recall at a fixed alert budget. `delay_days`, `on_time_in_full`, `delay_reason`, `delivery_note_clean` and `delivered_date` are recorded after delivery and give the model the answer.*

* MLQ-2 What will a returning customer spend on their next order?

*Regression · one returning customer’s next order · target: order\_total · temporal split*

*Figure 2 shows that order value varies strongly with product mix: Laptops generate AUD 2.75m from 1,397 units, while Accessories generate AUD 0.56m from 3,051. A regression model could predict a returning customer’s next order value from prior spending, purchase frequency, recency, category mix, channel history and segment. The prediction could support targeted recommendations or promotions before the next purchase. Evaluate with MAE against a customer’s historical-average baseline. To prevent leakage, all predictors must use only transactions before the target order; the target order’s items, price, discount and tax must be excluded.*

* MLQ-3 Which delivered items will attract a rating of 2 or below?

*Classification · one delivered item · target: `rating <= 2` · train on earlier orders, test on later*

Figure 8 showed rating falling from 3.879 in the cheapest price quintile to 3.548 in the fourth, about seven standard errors, then rebounding to 3.684 in the most expensive. Price and rating are related, but not in a straight line, so price is no rule on its own. A model would spot items at risk of a bad review right after delivery, in time to reach the customer first. At that moment we have product category and unit price, carrier, service level, delivery lateness, sales channel, and customer history computed only from earlier transactions. Score on precision and recall for the low-rating class against its 17.86% base rate — 1,250 of 7,000 — since accuracy would hide a minority class. Two risks: only 7,000 of 15,685 items are reviewed, so we learn only from people who chose to write; and every review-derived field is created with the rating, so all of them go.

* MLQ-4 What natural customer segments exist?

Clustering · one customer · no target · stability checked on random subsets

Figure 7 showed the four labels in customer\_segment only 1.5 standard errors apart on spend, while order frequency and basket size differ in opposite directions by about 2.4 each. The existing labels do not group people by how they buy. Data-driven groups would decide who gets an offer to order more often and who gets a bigger basket. Score on silhouette, and on whether the same customers regroup on random subsets. Risks: 500 customers may be too few for stable groups; features must be rescaled, or spend in the tens of thousands drowns an order count near ten; and groups that track postcode would price by address.

* MLQ-5 Which customers will order again within the next 30 days?

*Classification · one customer after an order · target: repeat purchase within 30 days · temporal split*

The dataset contains 5,000 orders from 500 customers across 2018, providing repeated purchase histories that can predict short-term return behaviour. A classification model could use previous order frequency, recency, spending, category mix, channel history, and customer segment to identify customers likely to order again within 30 days. This could prioritise retention offers rather than targeting every customer. Evaluate using precision-recall AUC and recall at a fixed campaign budget. All predictors must precede the prediction date, and exclude orders in the final 30 days because their outcomes cannot be fully observed.

# **6\. Limitations**

**One merchant, one year, one state.** The data contains 5,000 orders placed in 2018 by 500 customers, all in Victoria and in AUD. Seven columns have the same value in every row — currency, order\_status, delivery\_status, tax\_category, verified\_purchase, home\_state and home\_country. Since the data covers only one year, we also cannot separate seasonal patterns from longer-term trends. These findings may therefore not apply to other regions or years.

**The two source files probably came from the same system.** They never disagree on value: 3,259 keys appear in both files across the six tables, with zero field differences. In the orders table alone, 3,500 of the 10,000 values compared had different formats, but their content was the same. If two systems recorded the data separately, we would expect at least some differences. This match suggests nothing was damaged in transit, but it does not prove either file is correct, so we should not call this cross-validation.

**Where we found no difference, the sample size matters.** Figures 3, 4 and 7 all show results with little or no variation. In Figure 4, no Express group has more than 100 deliveries, giving a standard error of around three to five percentage points. This means a difference of that size may be too small for this design to detect. That is a good reason not to spend money on a change, but it does not prove the change would have no effect.

**Ratings only represent people who chose to write a review.** There are 7,000 reviews from 15,685 delivered items, measured at item level, so one order can appear more than once. Findings 2, 7 and 8 therefore describe reviewers rather than all customers. The customers who stayed silent may be exactly those a service-recovery programme would need to reach.

**Nothing here proves cause and effect.** Late deliveries have a higher average rating than on-time deliveries, 3.82 compared with 3.70. This unexpected result suggests that some unobserved factor may influence both. For example, a seller who ships slowly may also be one that customers tend to rate generously, and we cannot control for that here.

**Three pairs of columns contain the same information twice.** delivery\_note\_clean reproduces the delivery outcome; expedited\_delivery is service\_level re-encoded; and delivery\_experience matches on\_time\_in\_full across all 7,000 rows. Each could give a model the answer it is supposed to predict, so these columns must be deliberately removed from any machine-learning model.

# **7\. Conclusion**

These tables are consistent, reconciled and reproducible, and that is what they are good for — describing this year accurately. The descriptive results are the usable ones: order value is skewed enough that the average misleads, and the categories earning the most revenue are not the ones selling the most units. The operational results mostly show no effect, and they earn their place by showing where money goes on distinctions the data cannot support. Cause and forecast stay out of reach until there is a second year and cost data.
